11290620_48a528f1.text: The circuitry of the dentate gyrus (DG) of the hippocampus is unique compared to other hippocampal subfields because there are two glutamatergic principal cells instead of one: granule cells, which are the vast majority of the cells in the DG, and the so-called "mossy cells."

11290620_a475a601.text: Two studies provided evidence that mossy cells were glutamatergic, one anatomical and the second physiological. The first anatomical demonstration of glutamate immunoreactivity was made in Golgi-impregnated mossy cells (Soriano et al., 1994). The physiological study used hippocampal slices to impale mossy cells-which were confirmed to be regular-spiking, hilar, and had thorny excrescences-and simultaneously recorded from neurons in the granule cell layer until a monosynaptic connection was identified. That study showed for the first time that mossy cells produced unitary EPSPs in granule cells, supporting the hypothesis that mossy cells were glutamatergic (Scharfman, 1995).

11290620_9cf36a5f.text: The dentate gyrus is unique among hippocampal subfields because it contains two distinct types of glutamatergic principal cells: the numerous granule cells and the specialized mossy cells (Scharfman et al., 2013).

11290620_474153a1.text: Anatomical studies demonstrated glutamate immunoreactivity in Golgi-impregnated mossy cells, while physiological recordings showed that mossy cells produce excitatory postsynaptic potentials in granule cells, confirming their excitatory glutamatergic function (Scharfman et al., 2013)(Fredes et al., 2021).
